h2.ar: حدث من قبل: البحار قبل المسوح

en: In 2001 a team of scientists led by Jeremy Jackson brought together bones from archaeological sites, old records and modern surveys from coasts around the world. They found the same story again and again: people had emptied coastal waters of many large animals long before scientists began to count them.
Their lesson was simple. If we only measure today, we do not know what has been lost. To know what a healthy coast looks like, we have to ask the past, and the past often answers with bones.
ar: في عام 2001 جمع فريق من العلماء بقيادة جيريمي جاكسون عظامًا من مواقع أثرية وسجلات قديمة ومسوحًا حديثة من سواحل حول العالم، فوجدوا الحكاية نفسها مرة بعد مرة: لقد أفرغ الناس المياه الساحلية من كثير من حيواناتها الكبيرة قبل أن يبدأ العلماء بعدّها بزمن طويل.
وكان درسهم بسيطًا: إذا لم نقِس إلا الحاضر فلن نعرف ما الذي ضاع. ولكي نعرف كيف يبدو الساحل المعافى، علينا أن نسأل الماضي، والماضي كثيرًا ما يجيب بالعظام.

en: If the people of Tylos and of the Samahij house fished in the nearby bays, their leftovers are a sample of those bays as they were: which fish lived there, and how big they grew. That sample could tell the planters at Arad what a full mangrove bay once held.
Or the fish may have come from reefs and open water far from any mangrove. Identifying the bones would decide.
ar: إذا كان أهل تايلوس وأهل بيت سماهيج يصطادون في الخلجان القريبة، فإن بقايا موائدهم عيّنة من تلك الخلجان كما كانت: أي الأسماك عاشت فيها، وإلى أي حجم كبرت. وهذه العيّنة قد تخبر من يغرسون القرم في عراد بما كان يحمله خليج قرم مكتمل.
أو ربما جاءت الأسماك من الشعاب والبحر المفتوح بعيدًا عن أي قرم. وتحديد العظام كفيل بالحسم.

refs: Crawford, H. & Rice, M. (2000). Traces of Paradise: the archaeology of Bahrain 2500 BC–300 AD. I.B. Tauris.
Ramsar Sites Information Service. Tubli Bay (site 921).
Jackson, J. B. C. et al. (2001). Historical overfishing and the recent collapse of coastal ecosystems. Science 293, 629–637.

spec.te: Did Arad Fort Stand on a Sea Spring?
spec.ta: هل قامت قلعة عراد فوق عين بحرية؟
spec.desc: A connection between four records on this map. Arad Fort, a square fort with four round towers built in the late 15th or early 16th century, stood on a separate islet before land reclamation joined it to Muharraq; a trench filled from wells once surrounded it, and a Portuguese map of about 1635 shows it under siege. Fresh water from the Eocene aquifer that feeds Bahrain's land springs also rises through the sea floor, most numerously off Muharraq, and pearling crews took on water there. About 3 km away, Al Sayah Island was built in the sea around such a freshwater spring by the 7th–8th century AD. The idea: Arad's islet lay on or beside a point where the Dammam aquifer discharged under pressure, so that its wells drew aquifer water from below rather than from a thin lens of rainwater, and this is why a fort on a small islet could keep a water-filled trench and stay supplied during a siege.
spec.sig: If true, the sea springs that shaped Bahrain's pearling and its name also shaped where it was defended, and the site of Arad could help locate spring points now buried under reclaimed land around Muharraq.
spec.ev: Arad Fort: built in the late 15th or early 16th century, before the Portuguese occupation of 1622; a Portuguese map of about 1635 shows it under siege with inner and outer walls; a trench once filled from wells surrounded it; it stood on a separate islet before reclamation (Walls 1987). Submarine Freshwater Springs: fresh water from the same Eocene aquifer as the land springs rises through the sea floor, most numerously off Muharraq; an 1829 traveller described a spring in about three fathoms; location shown is approximate. Al Sayah Island: built in the sea around a freshwater spring, with a cistern and a water-raising mechanism, pottery of the 7th–8th century AD. Dammam Aquifer: Khobar and Alat limestones; most springs no longer flow naturally after abstraction. Map distances: Arad Fort to Al Sayah Island about 2.9 km; to the approximate submarine-springs marker about 5.4 km.
spec.an: On small, low islands in the sea, fresh groundwater usually exists only as a thin lens of rainwater floating on denser salt water, a relationship described by Herzberg (1901) and Badon Ghijben; such lenses are easily exhausted by heavy pumping. A well on a small islet that could keep a moat filled would therefore be unusual unless it was fed from below. On this same map, Al Sayah Island is a documented case of people building in the sea around a freshwater spring.
spec.val: Find the wells of Arad Fort and of its trench in the restoration records and on the ground; measure the salinity and chemistry of any water still in them, with strontium and other isotopes, and compare it with Dammam aquifer water and with sea water; core the trench fill for brackish- and freshwater microfossils such as ostracods and diatoms; survey the ground beneath the fort with geophysics for a karst opening or spring conduit; search old charts and oral accounts for springs (kawkab) near the former islet.
dlist: Rival explanation 1: the wells drew on a thin lens of rainwater under the islet, enough for drinking but not linked to the aquifer.
Rival explanation 2: the trench was in fact filled mainly by sea water through the wells or at high tide, and drinking water came from elsewhere.
Rival explanation 3: water for the garrison was carried by boat from springs on the main island or at sea, and the islet's own wells mattered little.
refs: Walls, A. G. (1987). Arad Fort, Bahrain: its restoration, its history and defences. Directorate of Tourism and Archaeology, Bahrain.
News of Bahrain. The land of two seas: the freshwater springs that made Bahrain.
Al-Noaimi, M. A. (2004). Development of water resources in Bahrain. PhD thesis, University of Plymouth.
Altuntaş, L. (2022). British archaeologists unearth the 1,200-year-old man-made island. Arkeonews, 13 February 2022.
Herzberg, A. (1901). Die Wasserversorgung einiger Nordseebäder. Journal für Gasbeleuchtung und Wasserversorgung 44.
spec.se: Arad Fort once stood on its own islet, ringed by a trench filled from wells, in the waters where Bahrain's sea springs are most numerous. Was the fort built over a spring? Nobody has tested this yet.
spec.sa: كانت قلعة عراد قائمة يومًا على جزيرتها الصغيرة، يحيط بها خندق يُملأ من الآبار، في المياه التي تكثر فيها عيون البحرين البحرية. فهل بُنيت القلعة فوق عين؟ لم يختبر أحد ذلك بعد.

spot.en: Born from a detail in one record and a pattern in others. The Arad Fort record says a trench filled from wells surrounded a fort on a separate islet. The submarine springs record says fresh water rises through the sea floor most numerously off Muharraq, and Al Sayah Island, about 3 km away, was built around exactly such a spring.
spot.ar: وُلدت الفكرة من تفصيل في سجل ونمط في سجلات أخرى. فسجل قلعة عراد يذكر خندقًا يُملأ من الآبار حول قلعة على جزيرة منفصلة. وسجل العيون البحرية يذكر أن الماء العذب يصعد من قاع البحر أكثر ما يصعد قبالة المحرق، وجزيرة السياح، على بعد نحو 3 كيلومترات، بُنيت حول عين من هذا النوع تمامًا.

title.en: The Fort That Drank From the Sea Floor
title.ar: القلعة التي شربت من قاع البحر

tag.en: A fort on a tiny islet kept a moat full of water. Where did the water come from?
tag.ar: قلعة على جزيرة صغيرة جدًا أبقت خندقها ممتلئًا بالماء. فمن أين جاء الماء؟

en: Arad Fort is square, with a round tower at each corner. It was built about five hundred years ago on a small islet, before reclaimed land joined it to Muharraq. A trench once ran all round it, and the trench was filled from wells. A Portuguese map of about 1635 shows the fort under siege.

A small islet in salty sea is a strange place to find enough fresh water to fill a moat. But off Muharraq, fresh water from Bahrain's great aquifer rises through the sea floor. Pearling crews once dived to the springs and filled goatskin bags with sweet water.
ar: قلعة عراد مربعة، في كل ركن منها برج مستدير. بُنيت قبل نحو خمسمئة عام على جزيرة صغيرة، قبل أن تصلها الأرض المدفونة بالمحرق. وكان خندق يحيط بها من كل جانب، يُملأ من الآبار. وتُظهر خريطة برتغالية من نحو عام 1635 القلعة وهي تحت الحصار.

والجزيرة الصغيرة في بحر مالح مكان غريب لتجد فيه ماءً عذبًا يكفي لملء خندق. لكن قبالة المحرق يصعد الماء العذب من خزان البحرين الجوفي الكبير عبر قاع البحر، وكان الغواصون يومًا يغوصون إلى العيون ويملؤون قِرَب الجلد بالماء الحلو.

en: Only about 3 kilometres from Arad lies Al Sayah Island. In 2022 archaeologists showed that it is not natural at all. People had built it in the sea, at least 1,200 years ago, around a freshwater spring, with a wall, a cistern and a machine for raising water.

Elsewhere in the world, small low islands usually have only a thin lens of rainwater floating on the salt water beneath. Such a lens runs out quickly. A spring fed from deep below is a different thing: it keeps giving.
ar: على بعد نحو ثلاثة كيلومترات فقط من عراد تقع جزيرة السياح. وفي عام 2022 أظهر علماء الآثار أنها ليست طبيعية أبدًا، بل بناها الناس في البحر قبل 1,200 عام على الأقل حول عين عذبة، بسور وصهريج وآلة لرفع الماء.

وفي أماكن أخرى من العالم لا تملك الجزر الصغيرة المنخفضة في العادة إلا عدسة رقيقة من ماء المطر تطفو فوق الماء المالح تحتها، وهذه العدسة تنفد سريعًا. أما العين التي تتغذى من الأعماق فأمر مختلف: إنها لا تكفّ عن العطاء.

en: If Arad's islet sat on a sea spring, its wells drew water from the aquifer itself, and the fort could hold a full trench and keep drinking through a siege. The water in its wells, or the mud in its trench, should still carry the signature of the aquifer.
Or the wells may have held only rainwater or sea water. A few samples could tell.
ar: إذا كانت جزيرة عراد قائمة فوق عين بحرية، فإن آبارها كانت تستقي من الخزان الجوفي نفسه، وكانت القلعة قادرة على إبقاء خندقها ممتلئًا وعلى الشرب طوال الحصار. وينبغي أن يحمل ماء آبارها، أو طين خندقها، توقيع الخزان حتى اليوم.
أو ربما لم تحمل الآبار إلا ماء المطر أو ماء البحر. وعيّنات قليلة كفيلة بالجواب.

spec.n: The Old Town and Its Springs
spec.te: Did the Old Town Fade With Its Springs?
spec.ta: هل خبا البلد القديم مع عيونه؟
spec.desc: A connection between four records on this map. Bilad al-Qadim was the main centre of settlement on the island in the 11th–13th centuries AD, and its excavated remains include medieval houses and water channels at the spring of Ain Abu Zaydan; its anchor monument, the Al-Khamis Mosque, was founded in the 11th century, given a second minaret about two centuries later and rebuilt in the 14th and 15th centuries. The area later became 'the old town' after Manama grew beside it on the coast, where Bahrain's harbour moved in the 19th century. Its record lies about 1.7 km from that of the Dammam aquifer springs, whose record calls the aquifer the hydrogeology behind the medieval towns. The idea: the rise of Bilad al-Qadim followed strong spring flow at Ain Abu Zaydan and its neighbours, and its slow loss of rank followed a weakening of that flow long before modern pumping, so that the medieval water channels hold a dated record of the springs.
spec.sig: If true, the water channels of Bilad al-Qadim would be the oldest dated measure of Bahrain's spring flow, a baseline for the aquifer that has lost almost 70% of its usable water, and a case where a town's fortunes can be read in its plumbing.
spec.ev: Bilad al-Qadim: main centre of settlement in the 11th–13th centuries AD; medieval houses and water channels at Ain Abu Zaydan; the Abu Anbra cemetery; named 'the old town' after Manama grew beside it; excavated by the Early Islamic Bahrain Project from 2001 (Insoll 2005; Insoll et al. 2016). Al-Khamis Mosque: 11th-century foundation with one minaret, second minaret about two centuries later, rebuilt in the 14th and 15th centuries, a section dated 1339. Dammam Aquifer and the Springs: springs used for over 4,000 years; called the hydrogeology behind Dilmun's temples and the medieval towns; most springs no longer flow naturally. Manama: on the northern coast, where the harbour moved from Qal'at al-Bahrain in the 19th century. Map distances: Bilad al-Qadim to the spring record's marker about 1.7 km, to the Al-Khamis Mosque about 0.6 km, to Manama about 3.6 km.
spec.an: No single study is cited here. In general terms, in dry lands where towns depend on springs, archaeologists and geologists have used the sediments of channels and pools, and the carbonate crusts that spring water leaves behind, to date changes in flow and to compare them with the growth and decline of settlements.
spec.val: Excavate and log the sediments in the water channels at Ain Abu Zaydan and any spring pools of Bilad al-Qadim; date them by radiocarbon on organic matter and U-series on spring carbonates; look for signs of falling flow such as silting, deepening or re-cutting of channels; compare the dated flow record with the building phases of the Al-Khamis Mosque, the houses and the Abu Anbra cemetery; compare with any dated spring deposits along the north coast.
dlist: Rival explanation 1: the town lost its rank because trade, pearling and the harbour drew people to the coast, while the springs kept flowing strongly.
Rival explanation 2: political changes on the island, not water, decided where the main town stood.
Rival explanation 3: the town only seems to fade after the 13th century because excavation has focused on its best-known centuries.
refs: Insoll, T. (2005). The Land of Enki in the Islamic Era: pearls, palms and religious identity in Bahrain. Kegan Paul.

Insoll, T., Almahari, S., MacLean, R. et al. (2016). Bilad al-Qadim revisited: recent archaeological research at the Al-Khamis Mosque, Ain Abu Zaydan and Abu Anbra, Bahrain. Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy.
Al-Noaimi, M. A. (2004). Development of water resources in Bahrain: a combined approach of supply–demand analysis. PhD thesis, University of Plymouth.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Manama, City of Trade, Multiculturalism and Religious Coexistence. Tentative List ref. 6354, submitted 20/07/2018.
spec.se: Bilad al-Qadim, the island's main town in the 11th–13th centuries, grew around springs and water channels, and later gave way to Manama on the coast. Did it fade as its springs weakened? Nobody has tested this yet.
spec.sa: نما البلد القديم، البلدة الرئيسية في الجزيرة بين القرنين الحادي عشر والثالث عشر، حول العيون وقنوات الماء، ثم أفسح المجال للمنامة على الساحل. فهل خبا مع ضعف عيونه؟ لم يختبر أحد ذلك بعد.

spot.en: Born from a coincidence of records on this map. The Bilad al-Qadim record lists medieval water channels at a spring. The spring record, less than 2 km away, calls the aquifer the hydrogeology behind the medieval towns. And the Manama record shows where the island's centre moved next: to the coast.
spot.ar: وُلدت الفكرة من تطابق سجلات على هذه الخريطة. فسجل البلد القديم يذكر قنوات ماء من العصور الوسطى عند عين. وسجل العيون، على بعد أقل من كيلومترين، يصف الخزان الجوفي بأنه الأساس المائي للمدن الوسيطة. وسجل المنامة يُظهر إلى أين انتقل مركز الجزيرة بعد ذلك: إلى الساحل.

title.en: The Town That Followed the Water

tag.en: Bahrain's medieval capital grew around springs. Its water channels may record why it faded
tag.ar: نمت عاصمة البحرين في العصور الوسطى حول العيون، وربما تسجل قنوات مائها سبب أفولها

en: Nine hundred years ago, the main town of the island was not Manama. It was a place now called Bilad al-Qadim, 'the old town'. Archaeologists have found its houses, its cemetery and its water channels at the spring of Ain Abu Zaydan. Its mosque, Al-Khamis, was built, enlarged and rebuilt from the 11th to the 15th century.

Less than 2 kilometres away is the record of the island's springs, fed by the great Dammam aquifer. That record calls the aquifer the hydrogeology behind the medieval towns. Later, the centre of the island moved to the coast, where Manama grew and the harbour settled in the 19th century.
ar: قبل تسعمئة عام لم تكن المنامة البلدة الرئيسية في الجزيرة، بل مكان يُسمّى اليوم بلاد القديم، أي البلد القديم. وقد وجد علماء الآثار بيوته ومقبرته وقنوات مائه عند عين أبو زيدان. أما مسجده، مسجد الخميس، فقد بُني ووُسّع وأُعيد بناؤه بين القرنين الحادي عشر والخامس عشر.

وعلى بعد أقل من كيلومترين يقع سجل عيون الجزيرة، التي يغذيها خزان الدمام الجوفي الكبير. ويصف ذلك السجل الخزانَ بأنه الأساس المائي للمدن الوسيطة. ثم انتقل مركز الجزيرة لاحقًا إلى الساحل، حيث نمت المنامة واستقر المرفأ في القرن التاسع عشر.

h2.en: Seen before: towns that lived by their springs
h2.ar: حدث من قبل: مدن عاشت على عيونها

en: In many dry lands, towns grew where springs flowed, and shrank when the water failed. Scientists who study them read two kinds of clues: the mud that settles in channels and pools, and the hard crusts that spring water leaves on stone.
Both can be dated. Put side by side with the dated buildings of a town, they can show whether the water fell first and the people left after, or the other way round.
ar: في كثير من الأراضي الجافة نمت المدن حيث جرت العيون، وتقلّصت حين نضب الماء. ويقرأ العلماء الذين يدرسونها نوعين من الأدلة: الطين الذي يترسب في القنوات والأحواض، والقشور الصلبة التي يتركها ماء العيون على الحجر.
وكلاهما يمكن تأريخه. وإذا وُضعا جنبًا إلى جنب مع مباني البلدة المؤرخة، أمكن أن يكشفا هل انخفض الماء أولًا ثم رحل الناس، أم حدث العكس.

en: If the old town followed its water, the channels at Ain Abu Zaydan should show strong flow in its great centuries and a fall afterwards, before or as people turned to the coast.
Or trade and the sea may have drawn the town away while the springs still ran full. The mud in the channels could tell which.
ar: إذا كان البلد القديم قد تبع ماءه، فينبغي أن تُظهر قنوات عين أبو زيدان تدفقًا قويًا في قرونه الزاهرة، ثم انخفاضًا بعدها، قبل أن يتجه الناس إلى الساحل أو في أثناء ذلك.
أو ربما جذبت التجارة والبحر البلدة بعيدًا والعيون ما زالت تفيض. وطين القنوات قادر على أن يخبرنا أيهما حدث.

spec.te: Were the First Mounds Built From the Cliffs?
spec.ta: هل بُنيت أولى المدافن من حجارة الجروف؟
spec.desc: A connection between four records on this map. At Wadi al-Sail, a wadi about 4 km long on the inland plateau, hundreds of 'Riffa type' cairn burials line the slopes; eight radiocarbon dates fall between 2300 and 1900 BC, and mounds of the same type were once scattered around Riffa, where Riffa Fort now stands on the cliff above the Hunanaiya valley. The Interior Basin record describes the rimrock of Eocene Dammam limestone that rings the centre of the island in cliffs more than 30 m high, with four members of different rock: a shark's-tooth shale, a brown crystalline limestone, an orange marl and a white limestone. The idea: the first mound-builders took their cairn stone from whichever rimrock member was exposed nearest to each grave, so that the stone of the earliest Dilmun mounds is a map of the local geology.
spec.sig: If true, the stones of the earliest Dilmun graves could be traced to particular beds and places, showing how far people carried stone for their dead, and giving a method to source the stone of the later mound fields of Hamad Town and Janabiyah.
spec.ev: Wadi al-Sail: hundreds of Riffa type mounds, mainly in the upper 3 km of the wadi; 266 possible mounds in the northern part; all excavated graves were cairn burials; eight radiocarbon dates of 2300–1900 BC; Mesopotamian and Umm an-Nar pottery (Gotoh et al. 2020; Abe & Uesugi 2021). Riffa type mounds were once scattered around Riffa but mostly lost to building. Interior Basin: closed basin ringed by Dammam limestone cliffs more than 30 m high; members of 9–15 m (shark's-tooth shale), about 33 m (brown crystalline limestone), 6–20 m (orange marl) and 6–62 m (white limestone) (Willis 1967). Riffa Fort: on the cliff between East and West Riffa, on the island's geological rim. Hamad Town and Janabiyah: each mound covers a central stone chamber inside a low ring wall. Map distances: Wadi al-Sail to Riffa Fort about 3.1 km, to the Interior Basin marker about 3.5 km, to the Hamad Town mound fields about 4.0 km.
spec.an: Nash, D. J. et al. (2020) used the chemistry of the sarsen stones at Stonehenge, England, compared with samples of sarsen from across southern Britain, to show that most of the stones came from one area about 25 km away (West Woods). Matching stone in monuments to its source bed by petrography and geochemistry is a standard method in archaeology.
spec.val: Sample stones from the excavated Wadi al-Sail cairns, and from mounds dug by the Bahrain Authority for Culture and Antiquities; build a reference set from each rimrock member along the wadi and the escarpment near Riffa; compare them by thin-section petrography, microfossils and trace-element chemistry; map each cairn's stone source and the distance to it; repeat for ring walls and chambers in the Hamad Town mound fields.
dlist: Rival explanation 1: the stone was gathered from loose rubble on the wadi floor, washed down by floods from many beds, so the cairns hold a mixture that matches no single nearby member.
Rival explanation 2: builders chose one preferred stone, for its colour or because it split well, and carried it from wherever it was found, regardless of distance.
Rival explanation 3: stones were taken from older graves and structures and reused, so the cairns record robbing and rebuilding rather than first quarrying.
refs: Gotoh, T., Saito, K., Abe, M. & Uesugi, A. (2020). Excavations at Wādī al-Sail, Bahrain 2015–2019. Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies 50, 171–187.
Abe, M. & Uesugi, A. (2021). Reconsidering the date of Riffa type burial mounds in the Early Dilmun period: new radiocarbon data from Wadi al-Sail, Bahrain. Al-Rāfidān 42, 75–85.
Willis, R. P. (1967). Geology of the Arabian Peninsula: Bahrain. U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 560-E.

Højlund, F. (2007). The Burial Mounds of Bahrain: social complexity in Early Dilmun. Jutland Archaeological Society.
Nash, D. J. et al. (2020). Origins of the sarsen megaliths at Stonehenge. Science Advances 6(31), eaba0756.
spec.se: The earliest Dilmun cairns line a wadi a few kilometres from the island's ring of limestone cliffs. Was each grave built from the cliff nearest to it? Nobody has tested this yet.
spec.sa: تصطف أقدم مدافن دلمون الركامية على جانبي وادٍ يبعد بضعة كيلومترات عن حلقة الجروف الجيرية في وسط الجزيرة. فهل بُني كل قبر من حجارة أقرب جرف إليه؟ لم يختبر أحد ذلك بعد.

spot.en: Born from a coincidence of records on this map. The Wadi al-Sail record says the oldest dated Dilmun cairns, the 'Riffa type', were once common around Riffa. The Riffa Fort record puts Riffa on the island's geological rim. And the Interior Basin record lists the four kinds of rock that make up that rim, all within a few kilometres of the graves.
spot.ar: وُلدت الفكرة من تطابق سجلات على هذه الخريطة. فسجل وادي السيل يذكر أن أقدم المدافن الركامية المؤرخة في دلمون، وهي من طراز الرفاع، كانت منتشرة يومًا حول الرفاع. وسجل قلعة الرفاع يضع الرفاع على الحافة الجيولوجية للجزيرة. وسجل الحوض الداخلي يعدّد أنواع الصخر الأربعة التي تتألف منها تلك الحافة، وكلها على بعد بضعة كيلومترات من القبور.

tag.ar: تقف أولى مدافن دلمون الركامية على مسافة قصيرة من أربعة أنواع من الصخر. فهل استعار كل قبر من أقربها إليه؟

en: More than four thousand years ago, people on the inland plateau of Bahrain began to bury their dead under heaps of stone. At Wadi al-Sail, a dry valley about 4 kilometres long, hundreds of these cairns line the slopes. Eight radiocarbon dates place them between 2300 and 1900 BC. Archaeologists call them the 'Riffa type', because such mounds were once common around Riffa.

A few kilometres away, the island's ring of cliffs rises more than 30 metres. Geologists have named four layers in it: a grey shark's-tooth shale, a brown crystalline limestone, an orange marl and a white limestone. Riffa Fort stands on the same rim. The stone was there. Did the builders simply use the nearest?
ar: قبل أكثر من أربعة آلاف عام بدأ الناس على الهضبة الداخلية في البحرين يدفنون موتاهم تحت أكوام من الحجارة. وفي وادي السيل، وهو وادٍ جاف طوله نحو أربعة كيلومترات، تصطف مئات من هذه المدافن على المنحدرات. وتضعها ثمانية تواريخ بالكربون المشع بين 2300 و1900 ق.م. ويسميها علماء الآثار طراز الرفاع، لأن مثلها كان منتشرًا يومًا حول الرفاع.

وعلى بعد بضعة كيلومترات ترتفع حلقة الجروف في وسط الجزيرة أكثر من ثلاثين مترًا، وقد سمّى الجيولوجيون فيها أربع طبقات: طفل أسنان القرش الرمادي، والحجر الجيري البلوري البني، والمارل البرتقالي، والحجر الجيري الأبيض. وقلعة الرفاع قائمة على الحافة نفسها. كان الحجر في متناول اليد، فهل اكتفى البنّاؤون بأقربه؟

h2.en: Seen before: the stones of Stonehenge

en: At Stonehenge in England, scientists wanted to know where the great sarsen stones came from. In 2020 a team of geologists and archaeologists compared the chemistry of the stones with samples of sarsen from across southern Britain.
Most of the stones matched one area, West Woods, about 25 kilometres away. Every rock carries a chemical fingerprint of the bed it came from, so a monument can be traced back to its quarry.
ar: في ستونهنج بإنجلترا أراد العلماء أن يعرفوا من أين جاءت حجارة السارسن الضخمة. ففي عام 2020 قارن فريق من الجيولوجيين وعلماء الآثار كيمياء تلك الحجارة بعينات من السارسن جُمعت من أنحاء جنوب بريطانيا.
فتطابقت معظم الحجارة مع منطقة واحدة هي ويست وودز، على بعد نحو 25 كيلومترًا. فلكل صخر بصمة كيميائية من الطبقة التي جاء منها، ولذلك يمكن تتبّع أي أثر حجري حتى محجره.

en: If the first Dilmun builders used the nearest rock, each cairn at Wadi al-Sail should match the layer exposed closest to it, and cairns in different parts of the wadi should hold different stone.
If instead the cairns all hold one favourite stone, or a random mixture, then people chose or gathered their stone in some other way. The graves themselves can answer.
ar: إذا كان أوائل البنّائين في دلمون قد استعملوا أقرب صخر، فينبغي أن يطابق كل مدفن في وادي السيل الطبقة المكشوفة الأقرب إليه، وأن تضم المدافن في أجزاء الوادي المختلفة حجارة مختلفة.
أما إذا ضمّت المدافن كلها حجرًا واحدًا مفضّلًا، أو خليطًا عشوائيًا، فقد اختار الناس حجارتهم أو جمعوها بطريقة أخرى. والقبور نفسها قادرة على الجواب.

spec.te: Was This Sea Ever Hotter Than Today?
spec.ta: هل كان هذا البحر يومًا أحرّ مما هو اليوم؟
spec.dr: c. 50 million years ago, compared with 1996–2017
spec.desc: A connection between three records on this map. The shark's-tooth shale, the lowest member of the Dammam Formation, is 9.1–15.2 m of shale and marl full of fossil shark teeth, laid down in the shallow Eocene sea that covered the region about 50 million years ago. A few kilometres away, the slightly older Rus Formation records restricted lagoons, sabkha pools and tidal flats along a narrow, storm-swept strait, with traces of evaporite salts. Offshore, the corals of Fasht Al Adhm are among the most heat-tolerant on Earth, yet bleached at 37.7 °C in 1996, at 38 °C in 1998 and after months above 34 °C in 2017. The idea: the shallow Eocene sea over Bahrain was at least as hot as the water of today's worst bleaching summers, and the chemistry of the shark teeth can measure it.
spec.sig: If true, Bahrain would hold a deep-time yardstick for today's Gulf heat, showing that this patch of sea has known such temperatures before; if false, today's heat would be beyond anything recorded in the island's own rocks.
spec.ev: Shark's-tooth shale: 9.1–15.2 m of grey to yellow shale and marl with abundant fossil shark teeth, on the inner slopes of the rimrock; shallow Eocene sea about 50 million years ago (Willis 1967). Rus Formation outcrop: Early Eocene, about 56–48 million years ago; restricted lagoons, sabkha pools, tidal flats, channels and storm washovers; 88% of 58 samples mainly dolomite; quartz pseudomorphs after gypsum and thin halite laminae (Amer et al. 2023). Fasht Al Adhm: bleaching at 37.7 °C (1996) and 38 °C (1998); in 2017 water above 34 °C from July to October cut nearshore hard-coral cover from 13.6% to 1.4% (AlMealla et al. 2024). Map distances: shark's-tooth shale to the Rus outcrop about 5.2 km, to Fasht Al Adhm about 32 km.
spec.an: No single study is cited here. In general terms, the ratio of oxygen isotopes in the hard enameloid of fossil shark and fish teeth is widely used as a thermometer for ancient seas, because enameloid resists change better than most shells. The method also depends on the isotope ratio of the sea water itself, which evaporation can shift.
spec.val: Collect shark teeth from several levels of the shark's-tooth shale; check each tooth for alteration by microscopy and trace-element and rare-earth analysis; measure the oxygen isotopes of the enameloid phosphate; estimate the isotope ratio of the Eocene water using the evaporite evidence from the Rus and any well-preserved shells or carbonates in the same beds; convert to temperatures and compare them with the 34–38 °C of the bleaching summers.
dlist: Rival explanation 1: burial fluids and the dolomitisation seen in the island’s Eocene rocks altered the teeth, so their chemistry no longer records the sea they grew in.
Rival explanation 2: the sharks lived mostly in deeper, cooler water and only shed their teeth here, so the teeth do not record the shallow sea over Bahrain.
Rival explanation 3: evaporation in a restricted strait changed the water’s own isotope ratio so much that tooth chemistry cannot be turned into a reliable temperature.
refs: Willis, R. P. (1967). Geology of the Arabian Peninsula: Bahrain. U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 560-E.
Amer, A., Skyttä, P., Ojala, A. & Heilimo, E. (2023). New insights into the depositional facies of the Early Eocene Rus Formation, Bahrain. Marine and Petroleum Geology 154, 106338.
AlMealla, R. K., Edullantes, B. & Hepburn, L. J. (2024). Bleaching threatens positive carbonate budgets on Bahraini reefs. Marine Biology 171, 39.
spec.se: Bahrain's corals bleach when the sea passes 34 °C, and a bed of 50-million-year-old shark teeth lies a few kilometres inland. Was the Eocene sea here even hotter? Nobody has tested this yet.
spec.sa: تبيضّ شعاب البحرين المرجانية حين تتجاوز حرارة البحر 34 درجة، وعلى بعد كيلومترات قليلة في البر ترقد طبقة من أسنان القرش عمرها خمسون مليون عام. فهل كان بحر الإيوسين هنا أشد حرًا؟ لم يختبر أحد ذلك بعد.

spot.en: Born from a coincidence of records on this map. The Fasht Al Adhm record measures how much heat the island's corals can take. The shark's-tooth shale record, about 32 km away on land, holds the teeth of animals that swam in an Eocene sea over the same place. And the Rus record next to it describes shallow lagoons and salt pools in a narrow strait, the kind of water that heats up fast.
spot.ar: وُلدت الفكرة من تطابق سجلات على هذه الخريطة. فسجل فشت العظم يقيس مقدار الحرارة التي تحتملها شعاب الجزيرة. وسجل طفل أسنان القرش، على بعد نحو 32 كيلومترًا في البر، يحفظ أسنان حيوانات سبحت في بحر من عصر الإيوسين فوق المكان نفسه. وسجل الرس بجواره يصف بحيرات ساحلية ضحلة وبركًا ملحية في مضيق ضيق، وهي مياه تسخن بسرعة.

title.en: The Teeth That Remember the Heat

tag.en: Bahrain's corals are running out of heat they can bear. Shark teeth from an older sea may say whether this place has been hotter
tag.ar: تقترب شعاب البحرين من آخر ما تحتمله من حرّ، وقد تخبرنا أسنان قرش من بحر أقدم هل عرف هذا المكان حرًا أشد

en: East of Bahrain, the corals of Fasht Al Adhm are among the toughest in the world. Still, in 1996 the sea reached 37.7 °C and they bleached. In 1998 it reached 38 °C. In 2017 the water near the shore stayed above 34 °C from July to October, and hard coral fell from 13.6 per cent of the reef to 1.4.

On land, about 32 kilometres away, lies a bed of shale full of fossil shark teeth, about 50 million years old. Those sharks swam in a shallow sea over the same place. Just below it, the Rus Formation describes lagoons and salty pools along a narrow strait. Shallow, salty water heats up fast. How hot was that sea?
ar: شرق البحرين تُعدّ شعاب فشت العظم من أصلب الشعاب في العالم. ومع ذلك بلغ البحر 37.7 درجة عام 1996 فابيضّت، ثم 38 درجة عام 1998. وفي عام 2017 بقي الماء قرب الشاطئ فوق 34 درجة من يوليو إلى أكتوبر، فهبط المرجان الصلب من 13.6 في المئة من الشعاب إلى 1.4 في المئة.

وفي البر، على بعد نحو 32 كيلومترًا، ترقد طبقة من الطفل مليئة بأسنان قرش متحجرة عمرها نحو خمسين مليون عام. سبحت تلك القروش في بحر ضحل فوق المكان نفسه. وتحتها مباشرة يصف تكوين الرس بحيرات ساحلية وبركًا مالحة على امتداد مضيق ضيق. والماء الضحل المالح يسخن بسرعة. فكم كانت حرارة ذلك البحر؟

h2.ar: حدث من قبل: أسنان تقيس الحرارة

en: A shark's tooth is covered with a hard, glassy layer called enameloid. As it grows, it takes in oxygen from the sea water, and the balance between heavy and light oxygen in it depends on how warm the water is.

Scientists around the world use fossil shark and fish teeth in this way to measure the temperature of ancient seas. There is one catch: if the water was very salty from evaporation, its own oxygen balance shifts, and that must be worked out first.
ar: تكسو سنَّ القرش طبقةٌ صلبة لامعة تُسمّى المينائين. وحين تنمو تأخذ الأكسجين من ماء البحر، ويتوقف التوازن فيها بين الأكسجين الثقيل والخفيف على دفء الماء.

ويستعمل العلماء في أنحاء العالم أسنان القروش والأسماك المتحجرة بهذه الطريقة لقياس حرارة البحار القديمة. لكن ثمة عقبة: إذا اشتدت ملوحة الماء بسبب التبخر تغيّر توازن الأكسجين فيه هو نفسه، ولا بد من حساب ذلك أولًا.

en: If the idea is right, the best-preserved teeth will show a sea of 34 °C or more, as hot as the summer that broke the reef in 2017.
If they show a cooler sea, then today's heat goes beyond anything the island's own rocks remember. Either answer would tell us something about the reef's future.
ar: إذا صحّت الفكرة فستكشف الأسنان الأحسن حفظًا عن بحر حرارته 34 درجة أو أكثر، أي بحرارة الصيف الذي حطّم الشعاب عام 2017.
وإذا كشفت عن بحر أبرد، فإن حرّ اليوم يتجاوز كل ما تتذكره صخور الجزيرة نفسها. وأي الجوابين سيخبرنا بشيء عن مستقبل الشعاب.

spec.n: The Reefs That Shelter the Meadows
spec.te: Do the Reefs Guard the Seagrass?
spec.ta: هل تحرس الشعاب مروج الأعشاب البحرية؟
spec.desc: A connection between four records on this map. Bahrain's reef flats (fashts) cover about 850 km², more than its land; on the largest, Fasht Al Adhm, branching corals are essentially gone after the bleaching of 1996, 1998 and 2017, and the nearshore carbonate budget, the balance between reef growth and erosion, has fallen to near zero. Around Mashtan Island, sandy beaches are ringed by seagrass beds and reefs, and Bahrain's largest seagrass beds run from south of Fasht Al Adhm to the Hawar Islands. That seagrass feeds the Gulf of Salwa dugongs, the world's second-largest population, as well as sea turtles, and shelters young shrimp and fish. The idea: Bahrain's reef flats break the waves and hold the sediment that keeps the seagrass beds behind them calm and clear, so as the reefs stop growing and wear down, the meadows nearest to them will be the first to thin.
spec.sig: If true, the loss of Bahrain's corals would reach the dugongs, a vulnerable species of global importance, through the seagrass, and protecting reef flats would also protect the meadows.
spec.ev: Fasht Al Adhm: reef platform of about 200 km²; reef areas total about 850 km²; Acropora cover 50–90% in 1988; bleaching in 1996 (37.7 °C), 1998 (38 °C) and 2017; nearshore hard-coral cover down from 13.6% to 1.4%; branching corals essentially gone; nearshore carbonate budget near zero (AlMealla et al. 2024). Mashtan Island: about 2.5 km² and 2.5 km offshore; sandy beaches ringed by seagrass beds and reefs; feeding area for dugongs and turtles and nursery for shrimp and finfish; three seagrass species; largest beds from south of Fasht Al Adhm to Hawar (Naser 2016). Gulf of Salwa: waters mostly under 10 m deep with Halodule and Halophila seagrass; herd of 674 in 1986; Bahrain surveys of 2006 similar to twenty years earlier (Preen 2004). Hawar Islands: dugongs and sea turtles feed on the seagrass beds. Map distances: Mashtan to the Gulf of Salwa marker about 28 km, Fasht Al Adhm to the Hawar Islands about 65 km.
spec.an: Ferrario, F. et al. (2014) brought together studies of coral reefs around the world and found that reefs reduce the energy of waves by an average of 97%, with most of it lost at the reef crest. Seagrass and other shallow habitats behind reefs therefore sit in much calmer water than open coasts.
spec.val: Place wave and pressure gauges in front of and behind reef flats around Mashtan and the southern fashts, and at open seagrass sites with no reef; measure turbidity and sediment movement; survey reef-flat height and rubble; map seagrass cover through time from satellite images and diver transects since the 1980s; test whether seagrass loss is greatest where reef flats have been worn down since the bleaching years.
dlist: Rival explanation 1: the seagrass is limited by heat and light, not waves, so the same heatwaves that bleach corals stress the seagrass directly, whatever the reefs do.
Rival explanation 2: dredging, reclamation and turbid water from coastal works, not reef loss, drive changes in the seagrass.
Rival explanation 3: dead reef flats keep breaking waves as rubble and rock for decades, so shelter lasts long after the corals die.

spec.se: Bahrain's reef flats have nearly stopped growing, and the seagrass beside them feeds one of the world's great dugong herds. Do the reefs keep the meadows calm? Nobody has tested this yet.
spec.sa: كادت مسطحات الشعاب في البحرين تتوقف عن النمو، والأعشاب البحرية بجوارها تُطعم أحد أكبر قطعان الأطوم في العالم. فهل تحفظ الشعاب هدوء المروج؟ لم يختبر أحد ذلك بعد.

spot.en: Born from a coincidence of records on this map. The Fasht Al Adhm record says the nearshore reefs have almost stopped building. The Mashtan record describes beaches ringed by seagrass beds and reefs together, and the largest beds running south from Fasht Al Adhm. And the dugong and Hawar records show who depends on those beds.
spot.ar: وُلدت الفكرة من تطابق سجلات على هذه الخريطة. فسجل فشت العظم يذكر أن الشعاب القريبة من الشاطئ كادت تكفّ عن البناء. وسجل مشتان يصف شواطئ تحيط بها مروج الأعشاب البحرية والشعاب معًا، وأكبر المروج ممتدة جنوبًا من فشت العظم. وسجلا الأطوم وجزر حوار يُظهران من يعتمد على تلك المروج.

pred.en: Waves will be clearly weaker behind Bahrain's reef flats than at open seagrass sites, and seagrass loss since the bleaching years will be greatest where the reef flats in front of it have been worn down the most.
pred.ar: ستكون الأمواج خلف مسطحات الشعاب في البحرين أضعف بوضوح منها في مواقع الأعشاب البحرية المكشوفة، وسيكون تراجع الأعشاب منذ سنوات الابيضاض أشد حيث تآكلت مسطحات الشعاب التي أمامها أكثر من غيرها.

test.en: Measure waves and turbidity in front of and behind reef flats and at open sites, survey the reef flats, and compare them with the seagrass record since the 1980s.
test.ar: قياس الأمواج وعكارة الماء أمام مسطحات الشعاب وخلفها وفي المواقع المكشوفة، ومسح مسطحات الشعاب، ثم مقارنة ذلك بسجل الأعشاب البحرية منذ الثمانينيات.

wrong.en: If waves behind the reef flats are no weaker than in open water, or if seagrass change shows no link to the state of the reefs in front of it, the idea fails.
wrong.ar: إذا لم تكن الأمواج خلف مسطحات الشعاب أضعف منها في الماء المكشوف، أو لم يظهر أي ارتباط بين تغيّر الأعشاب البحرية وحال الشعاب التي أمامها، تسقط الفكرة.

tag.en: Bahrain's reefs have almost stopped growing. The seagrass behind them feeds the dugongs. Are the two linked?
tag.ar: كادت شعاب البحرين تتوقف عن النمو، والأعشاب البحرية خلفها تُطعم الأطوم. فهل بينهما صلة؟

en: Bahrain has more reef than land: about 850 square kilometres of reef flats, called fashts. But after the hot summers of 1996, 1998 and 2017, the branching corals of Fasht Al Adhm are almost all gone, and the reefs near the shore have nearly stopped building new stone.

Not far away, around Mashtan Island, seagrass beds and reefs lie side by side. Bahrain's largest seagrass beds run south from Fasht Al Adhm to the Hawar Islands. They feed the dugongs of the Gulf of Salwa and the sea turtles, and shelter young shrimp and fish. What happens to the meadows when the reefs stop growing?
ar: في البحرين شعاب أكثر من اليابسة: نحو 850 كيلومترًا مربعًا من مسطحات الشعاب التي تُسمّى الفشوت. لكن بعد صيف 1996 و1998 و2017 الحارّ كادت المرجانيات المتفرعة في فشت العظم تختفي كلها، وكادت الشعاب القريبة من الشاطئ تتوقف عن بناء حجر جديد.

وغير بعيد من هناك، حول جزيرة مشتان، تقع مروج الأعشاب البحرية والشعاب جنبًا إلى جنب. وتمتد أكبر مروج البحرين جنوبًا من فشت العظم حتى جزر حوار، فتُطعم أطوم خليج سلوى والسلاحف البحرية، وتؤوي صغار الروبيان والأسماك. فماذا يحدث للمروج حين تكفّ الشعاب عن النمو؟

h2.en: Seen before: reefs that tame the waves
h2.ar: حدث من قبل: شعاب تروّض الأمواج

en: In 2014 a team of marine scientists gathered studies of coral reefs from around the world. They asked a simple question: how much of a wave's energy does a reef take away?
The answer was striking: on average, 97 per cent. Most of it is lost where the waves first break on the reef crest. Behind a healthy reef, the water is far calmer than on an open coast.
ar: في عام 2014 جمع فريق من علماء البحار دراسات عن الشعاب المرجانية من أنحاء العالم، وطرحوا سؤالًا بسيطًا: كم تنزع الشعاب من طاقة الموجة؟
وكان الجواب لافتًا: 97 في المئة في المتوسط، يضيع معظمها حيث تنكسر الأمواج أول مرة على حافة الشعاب. وخلف الشعاب السليمة يكون الماء أهدأ بكثير منه على الساحل المكشوف.

en: If Bahrain's reef flats shelter the seagrass, the waves behind them should be weaker than at open sites, and the meadows should thin first where the reefs in front have worn down.
If not, heat, light or coastal works may matter more than waves. Either way, the answer reaches all the way to the dugongs.
ar: إذا كانت مسطحات الشعاب في البحرين تحمي الأعشاب البحرية، فينبغي أن تكون الأمواج خلفها أضعف منها في المواقع المكشوفة، وأن تبدأ المروج بالتراجع أولًا حيث تآكلت الشعاب التي أمامها.
وإن لم يكن الأمر كذلك، فقد تكون الحرارة أو الضوء أو الأعمال الساحلية أهم من الأمواج. وفي الحالين يصل الجواب إلى الأطوم نفسها.
